title: Drona Passes Away (Day 15)
body:
Drona Passes Away (Day 15)

कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥

Translation: Your right is to perform your prescribed duty, but never to its fruits; let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. (Bhagavad Gita 2.47)

The fourteenth night did not bring the customary cease-fire; instead, the battle raged continuously in the eerie, flickering glow of thousands of torches. Ghatotkacha, Bhima's colossal asura son, unleashed a terrifying midnight campaign, moving through the air and destroying Kuru divisions with magical weapons. In his desperation to save his collapsing army, Karna was compelled to hurl the infallible Shakti spear—a divine weapon granted to him by Indra, which he had meticulously hoarded for his decisive duel with Arjuna—at the young giant. Ghatotkacha fell dead, but his massive body crushed an entire Kuru division as he fell, proving that even in death, the asura served Sree Krishna's grand cosmic design of neutralising Karna's ultimate weapon.
On the fifteenth morning, Acharya Drona, grieved by the endless carnage and the collapse of the moral code, nevertheless fought with devastating, unchecked fury. Sree Krishna recognised that as long as the preceptor held weapons, no force in the three worlds could defeat him. Sree Krishna revealed that Drona's only vulnerability was his doting attachment to his son Ashwatthama; if he were to believe his son had perished, he would renounce all interest in worldly life and lay down his arms.
Bhima slew a massive war-elephant named Ashwatthama, belonging to the King of Malava, and shouted across the battlefield that Ashwatthama was dead. Suspicious of the claim, Drona turned to Yudhishthira, whose reputation for absolute truthfulness was renowned across the earth. Pressed by Sree Krishna to perform this painful duty for the restoration of Dharma, Yudhishthira uttered the calculated words: 'Ashwatthama is dead,' adding in a low whisper, 'the elephant, not the man' (Ashwatthama hata, iti gaja).
At that moment, as the shadow of untruth touched Yudhishthira's tongue, his royal chariot, which had previously always glided four inches above the earth as a physical manifestation of his purity, sank heavily to the bare, bloody ground, making him of the earth, earthy. Believing his beloved son had perished, Drona was instantly overcome by intense detachment (Vairagya). He threw down his bow, sat in the Yoga posture of meditation on the chariot floor, and focused his mind on the Supreme Soul (Paramaathma). As his soul departed from his body, Dhrishtadyumna—who had been born from the sacrificial fire for the sole purpose of Drona's end—leapt onto the chariot and struck off the head of the non-combatant, meditating preceptor, throwing both armies into deep, agonising silence.
